content:
Moving keyboard shortcuts to a customizable macro keypad was the most efficient upgrade I've ever made.

Keyboard Shortcut Exploration Journey

I was first introduced to keyboard shortcuts through the simple text replacement feature in macOS — using @@ to type out my primary email address, and similar shortcuts for my full name, address, phone number, postal code, and so on.

After that, I decided to level up by using Keyboard Maestro to set shortcuts that directly open my most frequently used folders and applications.

From the desktop to the Downloads folder, and then to work-related folders, pressing Fn+F1 through Fn+F6 has become pure muscle memory, saving the trouble of clicking the mouse multiple times. The other function keys are used to launch commonly used applications and websites, as well as Keyboard Maestro's clipboard history switcher.

I went further to automate my workflows, including opening QuickTime and starting a new recording, as well as automatically launching ShurePlus MOTIV when a specific USB-C microphone is plugged in.

Soon I started customizing keyboard shortcuts for Adobe Audition's tools, settings, and panel configurations — some of which I immediately moved over to my Logitech MX Master mouse for even faster editing.

Taking It Further

This setup served me well for a long time, until one day my 9to5Mac colleague Gui Rambo introduced me to a small macro keypad he had purchased, with 12 buttons and 3 knobs. I immediately found it intriguing and bought the same model.

Right out of the box, I discovered it required additional configuration to work properly on macOS. Fortunately, there was a GitHub project that handled all the complex parts, and I let ChatGPT take care of the rest.

One major benefit of this setup is having a dedicated keyboard to trigger Keyboard Maestro shortcuts, so I don't have to memorize them, nor worry about ergonomic issues.

Even better, since this keypad can have up to 12 buttons per layer with a total of 3 layers, and the knobs can also be pressed as buttons, I can adopt one operation mode when using Adobe Audition, and a completely different mode when working at the operating system level.

When using Adobe Audition, this macro keypad working together with the MX Master mouse allows me to quickly switch tools, export files (or export only the selected portion), apply various effects such as volume normalization, compression, de-reverb, de-essing, ripple delete, and more — orders of magnitude faster than using standard keyboard shortcuts, let alone not using shortcuts at all, and the workflow is much smoother too.

At the operating system level, I can switch the same keypad to another layer and just as easily switch audio input, adjust volume, fine-tune screen brightness, mute and unmute the microphone, and open frequently used folders.

Honestly, it took me some time to memorize all these commands, but they became habits faster than I expected. More importantly, when I have to work in an environment without this setup, my Mac honestly feels broken.

Beyond all this, macro keypads come in a huge variety of shapes and sizes — shapes, sizes, buttons, knobs, lighting colors — you name it, it's out there. There really is a sense of endless exploration in this field. If your work involves any repetitive actions (and whose doesn't?), I wholeheartedly recommend giving it a try.
